issues.legal_issue: A state legislature may impose a tax directly on urban land by reference to its market value without legislating on the national power to tax the aggregate value of assets.
material_facts: The legislation imposed a tax on each urban landholding, calculated as a percentage of that land's market value.
The tax was imposed on the land as a unit and did not aggregate an owner's assets or calculate the owner's net wealth.
The constitutional challenge disputed the state legislature's authority to enact the tax and argued that a tax on land alone did not fall within its taxing authority over land and buildings.
issues.conclusion: The legislation was, in pith and substance, a tax on land within the state legislature's competence and did not trench on the national power to tax the capital value of assets.
issues.legal_principle: The legislative entries are broad categories to be interpreted liberally, and legislative competence is determined by the law's pith and substance. A tax directly on land as a unit differs from a tax on the aggregate value of an individual's or company's assets. The court relied on Ralla Ram v. Province of East Punjab, [1948] F.C.R. 207; Sudhir Chandra Nawn v. Wealth Tax Officer, A.I.R. 1969 S.C. 59; Gallahagher v. Lynn, [1937] A.C. 863; Subrahmanyan Chettiar v. Muttuswami Goundan, [1940] F.C.R. 188; Raja Jagannath Baksh Singh v. State of U.P., [1963] 1 S.C.R. 220; and H. R. S. Murthy v. Collector of Chittoor, [1964] 6 S.C.R. 666. The relevant constitutional subjects are List II Entry 49 and List I Entry 86.

rule.if: constitutional_challenge_to_state_land_tax and tax_imposed_directly_on_land_units and tax_measured_by_land_market_value and not tax_based_on_aggregate_asset_value

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_state_land_t: A party challenges the constitutional validity of a state legislature's tax on land.
predicates.tax_imposed_directly_on_land_units: The tax is imposed directly on each parcel or unit of land.
predicates.tax_measured_by_land_market_value: The amount of tax is measured by the market value of the land.
predicates.tax_based_on_aggregate_asset_value: The tax is calculated by aggregating the taxpayer's assets or determining the taxpayer's net wealth.

issues.definition: When a constitutional challenge concerns a tax imposed directly on land units and measured by their market value, rather than by aggregate asset value, the rule recognizes the state legislature's authority to tax the land.

issues.legal_issue: An individualized procedure for determining land market value, with an opportunity to provide evidence and challenge the assessment, does not make the valuation process arbitrary.
material_facts: The legislation required an owner to submit a return stating the land's extent and the owner's estimate of its market value.
The assessing officer could examine the return, seek evidence, and hear the owner before determining market value; a procedure also applied when an owner failed to file a return.
The legislation provided an appeal to a tribunal consisting of a judicial officer, revision in specified circumstances, and powers to receive evidence and require documents.
The assessment proceeding was judicial in character, and the officer was required to form an objective opinion based on relevant material.
issues.conclusion: The market-value determination provisions did not violate the guarantee of equality because they required an objective assessment through a judicially structured process.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 is not violated merely because an officer determines market value where the statutory language and procedure require an objective decision on relevant evidence. The court relied on sections 6, 7, and 9 to 11 for valuation and assessment procedures; section 20 for appeals; sections 30 and 32 for review and correction; and section 33 for powers relating to evidence and documents. The court also noted that the valuation function was judicial or quasi-judicial in character.

rule.if: constitutional_challenge_to_land_valuation_procedure and individualized_market_value_assessment and owner_can_present_relevant_evidence and assessment_must_be_objective and appeal_or_review_is_available

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_land_valuati: A party challenges the fairness of the procedure used to assess land for a tax.
predicates.individualized_market_value_assessment: The assessing authority determines the market value of each parcel of land rather than assigning a value based only on a broader zone.
predicates.owner_can_present_relevant_evidence: The owner has an opportunity to submit relevant evidence before the assessment is determined.
predicates.assessment_must_be_objective: The assessing authority must decide the value objectively on relevant material.
predicates.appeal_or_review_is_available: The assessment can be challenged through an appeal or review process.

issues.definition: The rule means that an individualized assessment based on an objective process, with an opportunity for the owner to present evidence and a means to challenge the result, is not arbitrary.

issues.legal_issue: A non-confiscatory tax measured by land market value is not shown to be an unreasonable restriction by combining it with a tax measured on a different basis.
material_facts: The challenged tax was calculated by reference to the market value of urban land.
An existing municipal property tax was calculated by reference to annual letting value.
The taxpayers argued that the combined taxes exhausted an unreasonably high proportion of property income.
The court held that the different bases of the taxes meant they could not be combined to assess the reasonableness of the challenged tax, and that the challenged levy was not confiscatory in effect.
issues.conclusion: The tax did not violate the right to acquire, hold, and dispose of property; the different taxes could not be clubbed together to establish an unreasonable burden, and the challenged levy was not confiscatory.
issues.legal_principle: The reasonableness of a tax is not governed by a narrow formula; legislative choices about the object and amount of taxation are generally matters for the legislature. A tax may be invalid where it is discriminatory, lacks procedural machinery, or is confiscatory or extortionate, but a tax that retains its character as a tax and is not confiscatory or extortionate generally cannot be challenged as unreasonable. Taxes based on different measures cannot be clubbed together to test the reasonableness of one of them. The court relied on Article 19(1)(f), Rai Ramakrishna v. State of Bihar, A.I.R. 1963 S.C. 1667; Kunnathat Thathunni Moopil Nair v. State of Kerala, A.I.R. 1961 S.C. 552; and Jagannath Baksh Singh v. State of Uttar Pradesh, A.I.R. 1962 S.C. 1563.

rule.if: constitutional_challenge_to_property_tax and challenged_tax_measured_by_land_market_value and other_tax_measured_by_annual_rental_value and challenged_levy_is_not_confiscatory

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_property_tax: A party challenges a property-related tax as an unreasonable restriction on the right to hold or deal with property.
predicates.challenged_tax_measured_by_land_market_v: The challenged tax is calculated by reference to the market value of land.
predicates.other_tax_measured_by_annual_rental_valu: Another tax relied on in the challenge is calculated by reference to annual rental or letting value.
predicates.challenged_levy_is_not_confiscatory: The challenged levy does not take property or operate as a confiscatory or extortionate exaction.

issues.definition: The rule means that a non-confiscatory land-value tax is not an unreasonable property restriction merely because it is challenged alongside a separate tax measured by annual rental value.

issues.legal_issue: Retrospective operation of a replacement tax law is not, by itself, an unreasonable restriction where the prior law imposed the same tax from that time and the replacement addresses the defect that invalidated the prior law.
material_facts: An earlier law had imposed the urban land tax from an earlier commencement date but was invalidated because it assessed land by reference to an average value for a sub-zone rather than the value of the particular land.
A replacement law omitted the sub-zone method and provided for tax based on the market value of each parcel.
The replacement law applied the tax from the commencement date of the earlier law, at the same rate.
The retrospective operation followed the earlier law's invalidation and was adopted to tax land from the date the earlier law had intended.
issues.conclusion: The retrospective imposition of the tax was not an unreasonable restriction in the circumstances.
issues.legal_principle: Retrospectivity is a relevant consideration in deciding whether a tax is reasonable, but it does not by itself make a law unconstitutional. The court relied on Article 19 and Rai Ramakrishna v. State of Bihar, A.I.R. 1963 S.C. 1667, and applied the legislative background of the replacement law, which corrected the defect in the earlier enactment while imposing the same tax from the earlier commencement date.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_retroactive_: A party challenges a tax law's application to a period before the replacement law was enacted.
predicates.replacement_law_cures_prior_defect: The replacement law corrects the defect that led to the invalidation of an earlier law imposing the tax.
predicates.prior_law_imposed_same_tax_from_that_tim: The earlier law had imposed the same tax from the period to which the replacement law applies retrospectively.
predicates.retroactivity_is_supported_by_legislativ: The legislative history shows that retrospective application was adopted to preserve the intended taxation from the earlier commencement.

issues.definition: The rule means that retrospective taxation is not an unreasonable restriction when a replacement law corrects the prior defect and the legislative background supports applying the same tax from the period covered by the earlier law.

issues.legal_issue: An objection to the method used to value a particular property does not, without more, invalidate the tax law or its general valuation machinery.
material_facts: A party objected to the use of the contractor's method for valuing a building on other property as a comparison in determining the value of the land under assessment.
The court held that this objection did not bear on the constitutional validity of the charging or machinery provisions.
The court stated that an owner could challenge a particular valuation through a statutory appeal or by seeking relief from a High Court.
issues.conclusion: The objection to a particular valuation method did not invalidate the tax law, while a challenge to the individual valuation remained available through the applicable appeal or writ process.
issues.legal_principle: A case-specific objection to the correctness of a valuation is distinct from a challenge to the constitutional validity of the taxing or assessment provisions. The court referred to the statutory appeal process and the High Court's jurisdiction to grant relief under Article 226.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_tax_law: A party seeks to invalidate the tax law or its general assessment provisions on constitutional grounds.
predicates.objection_concerns_particular_property_v: The objection concerns how the value of one particular property was determined.
predicates.individual_valuation_can_be_challenged_s: The taxpayer has a separate appeal or judicial process through which to contest the individual valuation.

issues.definition: The rule means that a challenge to a particular valuation does not invalidate the tax law when the individual assessment can be contested separately.
